procedural_history.impugned_order: Conviction under sections 353 and 506(1) of the Indian Penal Code.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State appealed the Magistrate Court's decision to the High Court under s. 417 of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High Court allowed the appeal and convicted Mangat Rai under s. 353 and s. 506 (1), sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment for four months on each count, the sentences to run concurrently.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Mangat Rai appealed to the Supreme Court, contending that the Act did not authorize forcible inspection of accounts and that the Inspector was exercising powers of seizure under s. 29(3) of the Act which he did not have. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

decision.appeal_result: the appeal fails and is dismissed

issue.issue_text: Whether a Sales Tax Inspector inspecting accounts under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, is entitled to remove an obstruction to the inspection of account books and whether in doing so, he is acting in the execution of his duties.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise inspection of his account books.
The appellant attempted to have the account books removed in a "clandestine manner" to prevent the inspection.
The Inspector tried to stop the removal by forcibly taking possession of the books.
In response, the appellant used criminal force against the Inspector to obstruct him.
law: Under Section 29(2) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958, all accounts of a dealer must be open to inspection.
Section 29(4) of the Act empowers the authorized officer to search any place of business for the purpose of this inspection.
Section 29(3) of the Act grants the power to "seize" account books, a power that the Inspector in this case did not possess.
application: The Court rejected the appellant's argument that inspection must be voluntary and that an inspector cannot use force. It reasoned that accepting this view would nullify the power of inspection, as any assessee could simply snatch away books to avoid scrutiny.

The Court distinguished the Inspector's actions from a "seizure" under Section 29(3). It held that the Inspector's goal was not to permanently dispossess the trader of the books, but to hold them temporarily for the purpose of inspection.

The Court reasoned that the power to inspect under Section 29(2) and search under Section 29(4) implicitly includes the power to get hold of the books to carry out the inspection. Otherwise, the power to search would be meaningless.

Therefore, when the Inspector saw the books and forcibly tried to take them to prevent their removal, he was not attempting an illegal seizure but was lawfully attempting to enforce his right of inspection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Sales Tax Inspector was acting in the execution of his duty when he tried to remove the obstruction to his inspection of the account books. The Court held that his attempt to forcibly take the books for temporary inspection was a legitimate part of his duty and did not amount to an unauthorized "seizure". Consequently, the appellant's argument was rejected.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection and prohibits any forcible inspection of accounts.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise check and wanted to inspect the account books.
When the inspector tried to prevent the clandestine removal of the books by forcibly taking possession of them, the appellant used criminal force against him.
law: Section 29(2) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act states that all accounts shall be open to inspection.
Section 29(4) of the Act empowers the Commissioner to search any place of business for the purpose of inspection.
Section 29(3) of the Act deals with the power to "seize" account books, a power the inspector in this case did not possess.
application: The appellant argued that the Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection and that the inspector's use of force was an illegal attempt to "seize" the books under s. 29(3).
The Court rejected this argument, stating that if inspection were purely voluntary, the power would be nullified, as any dealer could simply snatch away or hide books to prevent inspection.

The Court distinguished the inspector's actions from a "seizure." It reasoned that the inspector's goal was not to dispossess the trader of the books permanently, but merely to "hold the books for a temporary period for the purpose of inspection."

The Court concluded that the power to inspect under s. 29(2) and search under s. 29(4) implies the power to overcome obstruction. Therefore, when the inspector saw the books and forcibly tried to take them, he was lawfully enforcing his right of inspection, not attempting an illegal seizure.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's contention, holding that the power of inspection under the Act is not limited to voluntary submission. An inspector is entitled to overcome obstruction and use necessary force to inspect account books, and such an action for a temporary period does not constitute an illegal "seizure."

issue.issue_text: Whether the Sales Tax Inspector's attempt to take hold of the account books for inspection amounted to an exercise of the power of 'seizure' under Section 29(3) of the Act, a power he did not possess.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise check and wanted to inspect the account books.
When an attempt was made to remove the books, the Inspector tried to forcibly take possession of them for inspection.
The appellant argued that this action was an attempt to 'seize' the books, a power the Inspector did not have under Section 29(3) of the Act.
law: Under Section 29(2) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, all account books of a dealer are open to inspection.
Section 29(4) empowers the authorized officer to search the business premises for the purpose of carrying out the inspection mentioned in Section 29(2).
Section 29(3) provides a separate power of 'seizure', which involves taking the account books into possession and removing them from the assessee's premises.
application: The Court reasoned that the powers of inspection (s. 29(2)) and search (s. 29(4)) must be read together. The power to search for books for inspection implies the power to take hold of them.

It distinguished the Inspector's action from a 'seizure'. The Court defined 'seizure' under the Act as dispossessing the trader and taking the books away. In contrast, the Inspector's action was merely an attempt to hold the books for a temporary period for the purpose of inspection.
The Court noted that if an inspector could not forcibly hold books for inspection, any assessee could simply snatch them away, which would nullify the power of inspection granted by the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that the Inspector's attempt to take hold of the account books was not an exercise of the power of 'seizure' under Section 29(3). Instead, it was a legitimate action to enforce his right of inspection, and his object was to hold the books temporarily, not to dispossess the trader.

issue.issue_text: Whether a person obstructing a Sales Tax Inspector from inspecting accounts can claim the right of private defence.

facts: A Sales Tax Inspector visited the appellant's shop for a surprise inspection of his account books.
When the Inspector tried to inspect the books, the appellant's son attempted to remove them in a 'clandestine manner'.
The Inspector tried to forcibly take the books from the son to prevent their removal and complete the inspection.
In response, the appellant used criminal force against the Inspector to obstruct him.
law: Under Section 29(2) of the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, a Sales Tax Inspector has the authority to inspect a dealer's account books.
Section 29(4) of the Act empowers the Inspector to search the business premises for the purpose of inspection.
Section 46(h) of the Act makes it an offence to obstruct an inspector from performing their duties.
The right of private defence cannot be claimed against a public servant acting in good faith in the execution of their duty.
application: The appellant argued that the Inspector was attempting an illegal 'seizure' of the books, which he was not authorized to do, and therefore the appellant was entitled to use private defence.

The Court distinguished between 'inspection' and 'seizure'. It reasoned that the Inspector's attempt to take the books was not a seizure (permanent dispossession) but an act to enforce his right of inspection (temporary holding).

The Court held that the power to inspect would be meaningless ('nullified') if an inspector could not prevent someone from snatching away the books during an inspection. Therefore, the Inspector was acting lawfully in the execution of his duty.
The Court concluded that the appellant's son, by trying to remove the books, was committing an offence of obstruction under Section 46(h) of the Act.
Because the Inspector was acting lawfully and the son was committing an offence, the Court found that no right of private defence could arise for the appellant.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim of private defence, ruling that the Sales Tax Inspector was lawfully executing his duty to inspect the accounts. The appellant's attempt to obstruct this lawful duty by using criminal force was not justified, especially since the person he was 'defending' (his son) was in the process of committing an offence by preventing the inspection.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Sales Tax Inspector inspecting accounts under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, is entitled to remove an obstruction to the inspection of account books and whether in doing so, he is acting in the execution of his duties.
appellant_arguments: The Sales Tax Inspector's attempt to hold the boy and take the copy books was not in the discharge of his public duty.
If there is an obstruction to inspection, it may be punishable under s. 46 (h) of the Act, but the Sales Tax Inspector cannot do anything to forcibly inspect the accounts.
respondent_arguments: To accept the appellant's contention would be to nullify the power of inspection and search contained in the Act, as any assessee could simply snatch away books to prevent inspection.
The Sales Tax Inspector was acting in the execution of his duty when the appellant used criminal force against him.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Madhya Pradesh General Sales-Tax Act, 1958, only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection and prohibits any forcible inspection of accounts.
appellant_arguments: The Act contemplates voluntary submission to inspection and there cannot be any forcible inspection of accounts.
The Act does not authorize forcible inspection of accounts.
respondent_arguments: Allowing assessees to obstruct inspection by snatching away books would render the power of inspection under the Act helpless and ineffective.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Sales Tax Inspector's attempt to take hold of the account books for inspection amounted to an exercise of the power of 'seizure' under Section 29(3) of the Act, a power he did not possess.
appellant_arguments: The Sales Tax Inspector's actions were an attempt to exercise the power of seizure under s. 29(3) of the Act, a power he did not possess.
As the Inspector was not authorized to seize the books, his attempt to take them was not a discharge of his public duty.
respondent_arguments: The Inspector's action was not a seizure; he merely picked up books that were lying in the shop and did not take them by force. It was the appellant who used force to take them away from the Inspector.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a person obstructing a Sales Tax Inspector from inspecting accounts can claim the right of private defence.
appellant_arguments: The appellant was entitled to exercise his right of private defence of the person of his son.
respondent_arguments: No right of private defence arises because the son was committing an offence under s. 46(h) of the Act by obstructing the inspector.

statutes.act_name: Madras General Sales Tax Act (1 of 1959)

cases.case_name: Commissioner of Commercial Taxes v. Ramkishan Shrikishan Jhaver
cases.principle: A statutory provision authorizing an officer to inspect accounts and goods implicitly includes the power to search the premises to find them. Further, there is no rule that such provisions should be construed very strictly.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The statutory power to enter and search a premises for the purpose of inspection implies the authority to take possession of account books for that inspection. This act is distinct from a 'seizure', which involves taking the account books into possession and removing them from the assessee's control.
obiter: There is no rule that provisions like this should be construed very strictly.
If, indeed, he had retrieved them by force it may have been possible to urge that latter act of his amounts to seizure.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A Sales Tax Inspector's statutory power of inspection is not limited to voluntary submission by the assessee. To prevent the power from being rendered meaningless, an inspector is acting within the execution of his duty when he takes hold of account books for inspection, even if an assessee attempts to obstruct him. Such an act is an enforcement of the right to inspect, not an illegal 'seizure', and obstructing this lawful duty is an offense that negates any claim of private defense against the inspector.
legal_tests_applied: Purposive interpretation of statutory powers: The court analyzed the legislative intent behind the power of inspection, concluding it would be nonsensical if it could be easily thwarted by non-cooperation.

Distinction between 'inspection' and 'seizure': The court examined whether the officer's attempt to take possession of the account books amounted to a seizure or was merely an attempt to enforce his right of inspection.

Analysis of precedent (obiter dictum): The court identified a contrary observation in a previous case, Hazari Lal v. State of Bihar, as obiter dictum, allowing it to examine the question independently without being bound by that statement.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the Act only contemplates voluntary submission to inspection was rejected because it would 'be nullifying the power of inspection and search contained in s. 29(2) and (4) of the Act.'
The claim that the Inspector's attempt to take the books was an unauthorized 'seizure' failed; the court framed the action not as a seizure, but as an 'attempt to enforce his right of inspection.'

The claim to a right of private defense was dismissed because the son, whom the appellant was allegedly defending, 'was clearly committing an offence under s. 46(h) of the Act' by obstructing the inspector, and therefore 'no question of private defence arises.'
why_respondent_won: The court found that the Sales Tax Inspector 'was acting in execution of his duty' when he attempted to inspect the books and was obstructed.
The court accepted the argument that allowing an assessee to snatch away books would leave the Sales Tax Inspector 'helpless to do anything in the matter,' rendering the statutory power ineffective.
The court determined that the son's obstruction was an offense, which meant the inspector was lawfully discharging his duty and could not be lawfully resisted.
policy_considerations: To accept the appellant's contention would be to nullify the power of inspection and search contained in the Act, as any assessee could simply snatch away books to prevent inspection.

The court reasoned that there is 'no sense in the legislature giving power to the empowered officer to enter the offices, etc., for the purpose of inspection' if the officer could not actually inspect the accounts found therein.

Allowing obstruction would mean an assessee who finds that the 'Sales Tax Inspector has got hold of a book, which might prove damaging to his case... could snatch away or ask his clerk or son or relation to snatch away the book and run away leaving the Sales Tax Inspector helpless.'
